verses.text: So then, since we’re surrounded by such a huge crowd of witnesses, let’s throw off everything that weighs us down, especially the sin that so easily traps us. Let’s run with endurance the race set before us,
keeping our eyes on Jesus, the pioneer and perfecter of faith. For the joy ahead of him, he endured the cross, ignoring its shame, and sat down at the right hand of God’s throne.
Think carefully about him, who endured such hostility from sinners, so you don’t grow tired and give up.
In your struggle against sin, you haven’t yet resisted to the point of shedding your blood.
And you’ve forgotten the encouragement that speaks to you like children: “My child, don’t take the Lord’s discipline lightly, and don’t give up when he corrects you.
For the Lord disciplines the one he loves and corrects every child he welcomes.”
Endure hardship as discipline: God is treating you as his children. What child isn’t disciplined by a parent?
If you aren’t disciplined—which everyone receives—then you aren’t legitimate children; you aren’t really part of the family.
We had human parents who disciplined us, and we respected them. Shouldn’t we submit even more to the Father of spirits and live?
Our parents disciplined us for a short time as they thought best, but God disciplines us for our good, so we can share in his holiness.
No discipline feels good at the time; it’s painful. But later it produces a peaceful harvest of righteousness in those trained by it.
So strengthen your tired hands and weak knees.
Make straight paths for your feet, so what is weak won’t be injured but will be healed.
Make every effort to live in peace with everyone and to be holy. Without holiness no one will see the Lord.
Make sure no one misses God’s grace, and don’t let a bitter root grow up and cause trouble, poisoning many.
Make sure no one is sexually immoral or godless like Esau, who traded his birthright for one meal.
You know that afterward, when he wanted the blessing, he was rejected. He found no chance to change his father’s mind, even though he begged with tears.
You haven’t come to a mountain you can touch, blazing with fire, darkness, gloom, and storm.
You haven’t heard a trumpet blast and a voice speaking words that made the hearers beg for no more.
They couldn’t bear the command: “Even if an animal touches the mountain, it must be stoned.”
The sight was so terrifying that Moses said, “I’m trembling with fear.”
Instead, you’ve come to Mount Zion, to the city of the living God, heavenly Jerusalem, and countless angels celebrating together.
You’ve come to the gathering of God’s firstborn, whose names are written in heaven. You’ve come to God, the judge of everyone, and to the spirits of righteous people made complete.
You’ve come to Jesus, mediator of a new covenant, and to sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than Abel’s.
Be careful not to refuse the one who speaks. If those who rejected the warning on earth didn’t escape, how much less will we escape if we turn away from the one who warns us from heaven?
Back then his voice shook the earth, but now he has promised: “Once more I’ll shake not only the earth but also the heavens.”
The words “once more” show that what can be shaken will be removed—created things—so that what can’t be shaken will remain.
So, since we’re receiving a kingdom that can’t be shaken, let’s be thankful and worship God acceptably, with reverence and awe,
because our God is a consuming fire.
